author: FakePlasticTrees@fedibird.com
text: 『オデュッセイア』を観た。 ホメロスの叙事詩なんてまったく読んだことなく、藤村シシンさんがアトロクで解説していた「ゼウスの掟」だけを頭に入れて観に行った。そういう素人にも分かりやすくエンターテイメント作品として面白かった（きっと原作をだいぶ省略したのだろうとは思うけれど）。 これといって特徴ないからこそ重宝されるのかもしれない、マット・デイモン。ディカプリオ同様、ほんとうにいい感じにオジサンになった…。盲目のエウマイオス、ジョン・レグイザモだったとは。ティボルトの印象が強すぎて衝撃。ロバート・パティンソン、意地悪そうな顔つきで怖い。あんなのに結婚を迫られてるアン・ハサウェイが気の毒。 ゼウスの掟を知っておいてよかった、と書いたが、つまりストーリー全体を通してオデュッセウスがトロイア戦争で「ゼウスの掟」を破ってしまったことの罪悪感にさいなまれ続けていた、ということか？アテナのブローチを終始握りしめる自分が、アテナの神殿で殺戮を指揮してアテナ像（と巫女）の首を刎ねるという倒錯。 知識があれば、セイレーンのところとか、渦潮（？）と海峡に出てきた巨大な手とかについてももっと楽しく観ることができたと思う。 #映画 #theodyssey #オデュッセイア

author: dbattistella@mstdn.ca
text: When the Roman emperor Tiberius turned a cave on the coast between Rome and Naples, into a private dining hall, the Odyssey was already about 700 years old. At the deepest point of the cave Tiberius placed a massive marble sculpture that showed the moment when Odysseus blinds the Cyclops, Polyphemus, a one-eyed man-eating giant. In 26 AD, while Tiberius was dining there, rocks fell from the roof of the grotto, crushing several of his attendants and nearly killing the emperor. In that collapse, the great marble figures were smashed, and there they lay, at the bottom of the cave, until 1957, when workers building a coastal road cut into the ground and found them. Slowly, piece by piece, the scene was meticulously put back together, and the sculptures now reside at the Sperlonga Archaeological Museum. #TheOdyssey #GreekMythology #RomanHistory #Art #Sculpture #Archeology

Me ha dado la completa sensación de estar frente a un antes y un después en la historia del cine como evento colectivo, como ya ni recordábamos que la gran pantalla podía volver a ser eso, GRANDE; el hábitat natural donde vivir el CINE con mayúsculas, en lugar de en el salón de nuestra casa. Tan importante, o incluso más, que su apabullante envoltorio de cine de fantasía mitológica (también de cine de terror, dadas muchas de sus escenas) y su demoledor diseño sonoro, es el contenido político y humanista que Nolan nos ha colado (casi) sin avisar, tan tristemente actual que conmueve y remueve todo. text: We went and saw The Odyssey this morning in Lower Hutt. First time I've been to the cinema for ages so it felt almost like a new experience. (My, the buckets of popcorn are large these days!) You can only but admire the scale and execution of The Odyssey as a film. Some scenes are absolutely amazing in the way they are portrayed on the screen, especially the one with the Cyclops. But the film is rather charmless in many ways. I felt it was hard to become engrossed in it as I was conscious I was watching something to admire rather than something to love. I can see why many people want to read the original after seeing the film. Not only would certainly help to make sense of it, especially as in my case, you were unfamiliar with the overall arch of the story. But also because I suspect the reading the The Odyssey would be more immersive and ultimately more satisfying. I am glad I saw the film but it is not one I would want to see again. #TheOdyssey

author: Gotterdammerung@glitch.social
text: Second, Nolan's use of #xenia in #TheOdyssey is one of the film's smartest ideas. Also where he becomes most historically & mythologically neat. In Homer, hospitality is one of the poem's structural laws. Zeus as Zeus Xenios protects guests & guest-friendship. The suitors violate xenia by consuming another man's household. Polyphemus violates it by consuming the guests themselves. The Phaeacians embody it by welcoming a stranger before they know who he is. #Odyssey

author: Gotterdammerung@glitch.social
text: A few comments on Nolan's #TheOdyssey Nolan having Odysseus say "the end of the Bronze Age" is worse than an anachronism. It briefly turns the myth into a documentary narrated from the future. "Bronze Age" is a modern archaeological category. Odysseus didn't know he was living in one, much less at its end. Roughly like a Roman in 476 CE announcing the end of the Western Roman Empire & welcoming the Early Middle Ages. Impressive historical awareness. Suspiciously good historiography.

text: The Odyssey, a quick review A few points about The Odyssey, though I know I’m a bit late on this… The Odyssey has quite a few qualities going for it, sure, but there has been a lot of talk surrounding it and some pundits got it right. There are genuine issues with it, from the changes made to the original material to the story-telling and the dialogue… I mean just to name a few things: The choices for the armour were quite odd and felt very much out of place for a story set in the late Bronze age. For anyone even remotely familiar with the subject, the Iron Age weapons, the armour and, among other things, the usage of war chariots, will surely feel anachronistic.What also baffled me was the pacing of the story. author: warnercrocker.com@warnercrocker.com
text: The Odyssey: A Review Have you ever had one of those moments in life that at the time felt like a great victory, but then turned sour later on, leading to regret? I have. It’s no fun to look back on. It can hurt worse to look in the mirror. Sure you can go into therapy to help you feel better about your choices and the ramifications. But first you have to face them, own them, and accept responsibility. Or you could try to bury them in the bottle. Or drugs, illicit or otherwise. Or some other way of trying to keep them from resurfacing. Or you could just throw up your hands, blame the gods. Perhaps defy them. But in the end the choices you make define you. How you deal with the definition tells your story. That’s essentially the story of Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey. Much the same as it was with Oppenheimer. Do a thing. Do it well. Succeed. Then realize what you’ve done has unleashed problems bigger than the one you set out to overcome. Is The Odyssey a good film? In my opinion, yes.

text: How Nolan’s Odyssey Departs From Canon Firstly, there are no cannons in Nolan’s The Odyssey. There are cannons in Dunkirk, and both films involve soldiers running around on beaches and being stuck in confined spaces, so it’s an easy mistake to make. Aside from that, how does Nolan’s vision depart from the longer-established understanding of this epic story? Together we can explore some of the differences and consider why the famous director chose to make these choices. The sequence with the magical bag of winds is not in the film, and the god Poseidon/Neptune never appears. Neither does his daughter Mindy. Also, after escaping from the Cyclops, the heroes are not aided by David Hasselhoff.Nolan also omits the wordplay in the Cyclops section where the seafarer picks a name that means “no name”. text: Notes after a second viewing of The Odyssey: • The most emotional moments for me were scenes with Eumaeus or Argus • The most powerful scenes involved an opening and a closing: the opening of Troy's gates and the closing of Penelope's chamber doors. Together, they also bookend the journey of Odysseus. • The music of Ludwig Göransson didn't overpower the important scenes but elevated them, which is the epitome of what a film score should do. The incorporation of instruments from antiquity was also seamless and quite ingenious. • Recognised actor Logan Marshall-Green which I somehow missed in the first viewing • It actually is a very straightforward journey story, but richly layered with themes. text: The Odyssey | Movie Review I got to go see The Odyssey on opening weekend, and it ruled. You should absolutely go see this movie if you think you might enjoy it. It’s one of my favorite Christopher Nolan films. The movie is gorgeous. You could see the work put into every single scene to make it come to life. Every time they were at sea, I was just mesmerized with how beautiful everything looked. Everything looked like it was the “same world”, and it felt “real” and mythical at the same time. The casting was great. The two people that took me a second to adjust to in their roles were John Leguizamo and Charlize Theron. author: aenthology@larkspur.one
text: FILM REVIEW - THE ODYSSEY 👥 Director(s): Christopher Nolan 🌍 Where: Cinema 🖊️ score: 9/10 Christopher Nolan has really made this film feel like a myth come to life. So many scenes in this were stunning, combined with the excellent acting and the soundtrack. It all comes together almost perfectly, especially in the flashback scene near the end. The only thing, genuinely the only thing that irked me in the whole film, was the accents. Because it felt like a myth come to life, the accents really stand out in a dissonant way, because the American accent sounds new. There are many languages and accents that sound old, but that specific one sounds new, and so it just felt a little off. Not because I want this film to be authentic or historically accurate (it's not real) but it didn't fit the theme or vibe of the film I guess? Not sure how to explain it but that's my only criticism. Other than that it was incredible! #Movie #MovieReview #Film #FilmReview #ChristopherNolan #TheOdyssey

text: #奥德赛 #TheOdyssey 这版电影可以说是诺兰解读版《奥德赛》：在卡吕普索的奥吉吉亚岛上吃莲花失忆七年的奥德修斯（《记忆碎片》）终于想起了妻子和孩子（《盗梦空间》），决定回家。在伊萨卡岛上，忒勒玛科斯学艺练武（《侠影之谜》），出门寻找父亲。奥德修斯扮成乞丐回到伊萨卡，杀死求婚人，回忆木马屠城（《奥本海默》），最后跟妻子一起航向日落，过上退休生活（《黑暗骑士崛起》）。 之所以说这是诺兰解读版，不仅仅是因为很多地方带着他以往作品的影子，也是因为他对原著里很多主题做了延伸性解读。其中最重要的就是荷马的《奥德赛》中心主题：Xenia，古希腊的待客之道。书中不仅有正面例子（例如送奥德修斯回伊萨卡的费阿克斯人），还有反面例子（所有奥德修斯航行中遇到的奇怪生物和人）。延伸性解读的地方在于，Xenia只要求友好待客，并没有“己所不欲勿施于人”这一条，而且我觉得奥德修斯把这一条准则放到特洛伊战争上也很奇怪，都打仗了还有什么待客之道。奥德修斯在扮成乞丐见妻子的时候说他帮忙打赢了特洛伊战争却造成古希腊礼崩乐坏，我觉得他这也未免太太高自己了。这里纯粹就是诺兰的奥本海默式解读。 电影里甚至保留了荷马一些固定搭配的形容，比如忒勒玛科斯总是说他能看到别人有雅典娜的眼睛，荷马一般形容雅典娜是“目光炯炯的女神”，或者称她为“灰眼睛女神雅典娜”。另一个巧妙的地方是，雅典娜经常变身成凡人，例如开头给忒勒玛科斯建议的门忒斯就是她变成的。 食莲人的改编也很巧妙，一开始卡吕普索叫奥德修斯别吃莲花了我就意识到这里用上了失忆梗，但诺兰实在太喜欢失忆了。 特洛伊的木马的设计确实也别具一格，后腿和尾巴支撑起直立的骏马，让我想起《伊利亚特》里，给伊利昂的固定形容词之一就是“饲养良马的”。我最近才知道诺兰当时拒绝导演《特洛伊》的机会，这个木马的设计就是在那个时候埋下的。不过电影里说这是给雅典娜的献祭我就觉得过于离谱：一方面马的创造者是波塞冬，希腊联军出航前给海神献祭比较合理；另一方这个礼物要让特洛伊人接受，而特洛伊人的守护者是阿波罗和波塞冬（两位神祇在战争期间都帮助特洛伊人，伊利昂的城墙就是他们建的），怎么说都和雅典娜扯不上关系。不过木马屠城的过程倒是很写实，所有人都没有穿盔甲，毕竟特洛伊人在那鼓捣一番马就能听见叮叮哐哐的响声了。 诺兰居然在西农这个角色上下功夫我也没想到，我觉得在叙事上串起安提诺俄斯虽然不符合原

author: tsupasat@infosec.exchange
text: My review of The Odyssey: I loved the historical realism (excepting the mythical creatures). You definitely felt the temple to Athena at Pylos might have looked like that. Metal was all bronze, not iron. The rhapsodes would pound sticks on the floor when declaiming a poem. I really appreciate attention to details like that. The movie also used the historical context of the poem itself as one of the themes. When Homer wrote The Odyssey, the age of the Trojan War (~1,000 BC) felt like a sort of golden age. Homer's time was a sort of Dark Age (~800 BC). Odysseus feels that he's played a part in this. There's a dark reference to the "Sea People" who might have been Phoenicians but it turns out the Greeks themselves behave like the very thing that they dread. Acting of course was brilliant. It was a long movie, but nothing felt unnecessary. Not appropriate for kids as there are very creepy parts (Circe, Cyclops). #theodyssey

author: Bad@hsnl.social
text: Nolan's Odyssey is a masterclass in storytelling. It is more Nolan than it is Virgil, more Virgil than it is Homer, yet it feels like the truest, purest adaptation of the ancient oral tradition that has traveled three millennia to appear on our screens. The story of Odysseus is not a fairy tale about travels, wars, and gods, as it is usually presented to us. It is and has always been a grounded horror story about living in fear of the unknown. The biggest and scariest of all unknowns being, how does someone who's awakened to the evils of society continue living within it? Where do we fit? It's been an hour and I still remember every story beat, every minor character, the anxiety inducing sound design and the distressing cinematography. Many were doubting the set designs, the costumes, the tone and the casting. Go watch it and be proven wrong. Agamemnon was on screen for less than a minute in total, yet you will remember his silhouette for the rest of your life. I already want to rewatc

text: What is myth? Is it an embellished version of historical events, or a symbolic language created by humans to tell the truth? I think the biggest problem with Troy begins right here. The film tried to make Homer "rational." It removed the gods, toned down the prophecies, and reduced the sense of fate. The result is a well-made film about an ancient war, but the spirit of the Iliad is missing. Because in Homer's world, the question is not a simple "Did the Trojan War happen?" The real issue is the bargain between glory and death, man's insignificance in the face of fate, whether anger makes a person divine or animalistic, and the fact that heroism is actually a curse. Now consider: What happens when you remove the gods? Poseidon is no longer the sea, only bad weather. Athena is no longer wisdom, but "strategic thinking." author: randywalters@sunny.garden
text: Last night, I finished reading *The Odyssey* … and though I haven’t read other versions for comparison, Emily Wilson’s translation is *spectacular*. This is the one to get. The language is contemporary, clear, and brilliant. All the way through, I found myself thinking about everyone who will be seeing Christopher Nolan’s film this summer. Ancient as the story is, there is much that speaks directly to our time … [a spoiler alert is unnecessary, after nearly 3,000 years] it ends with Zeus hurling a thunderbolt, and the goddess Athena shouting “Stop this war!” Hard to miss the point, these days … The momentum of the final chapters was incredible. I found myself thinking … “you know, I really hope that Nolan took the time to sit down with Quentin Tarantino for at least a drink and a chat …” because there’s a climactic sequence that struck me as being pure Tarantino. Still, I can’t wait to see how Nolan pulls this off; I believe he will, and if he does, he has to be a shoo-in for Best Adap

text: Jason (& the Argonauts) Jason was an ancient Greek mythological hero & leader of the Argonauts, whose quest for the Golden Fleece is in Greek literature.He’s the son of Aeson, who was the rightful King of Iolcos (modern-day Vollos). He was married to the “sorceress” Medea, the granddaughter of Helios, the sun god. Jason appears in various literary works in the classical world of Greece & Rome, including the epic poem Argonautica & the tragedy Medea. Pelias (Jason’s half-uncle & his dad’s half-brother) was power hungry & sought to gain authority over all of Thessaly. Pelias was the offspring of a union between their shared mom, Tyro (the daughter of Salmoneus), & the sea god, Poseidon. In a bitter feud, Jason overthrew Aeson (again, who was the rightful King), killing all the descendants of Aeson that he could. He spared his half-brother for unknown reasons.
